title: Antecedents and correlates of improved cognitive performance in children exposed in utero to low levels of lead.
ehr_evidence: Data came from a prospective birth cohort followed longitudinally by the research team, with capillary/venous blood samples collected at 6, 12, 18, 24, and 57 months and cognitive assessments administered at 24 and 57 months; no electronic health record, claims, or registry database was used.
summary: A prospective longitudinal cohort study of children followed from birth examining correlates of change in cognitive performance (z-score change between 24 and 57 months) in relation to prenatal (cord blood lead) and postnatal lead exposure and sociodemographic factors.
key_findings: Cord blood lead level (continuous) was positively associated with change in performance (Δz), coefficient 0.03, SE 0.01, p=0.003 unadjusted and 0.03, SE 0.01, p=0.016 adjusted for MDI at 24 months.
Higher postnatal blood lead at 18 months was inversely associated with Δz (coefficient -0.22, SE 0.09, p=0.018 unadjusted; -0.21, SE 0.08, p=0.007 adjusted).
Higher blood lead at 24 months was inversely associated with Δz (coefficient -0.23, SE 0.09, p=0.012 unadjusted; -0.22, SE 0.08, p=0.005 adjusted).
Higher HOME score was associated with greater improvement (coefficient 0.07, SE 0.01, p=0.0001 adjusted).
Higher social class was associated with greater improvement (coefficient -0.22, SE 0.06, p=0.0002 adjusted).
Higher maternal IQ was associated with greater improvement (coefficient 0.01, SE 0.00, p=0.003 adjusted).
Gender was not significantly associated with Δz (coefficient 0.18, SE 0.12, p=0.13 adjusted).
Ethnicity was not significantly associated with Δz after adjustment (coefficient 0.15, SE 0.27, p=0.57 adjusted).
Among children with high cord blood lead, the net gain in performance between 24 and 57 months was 6.1 points (7.0-0.9), a substantial percentage of their relative deficit (7.8 points) at 24 months.
Among children with high cord blood lead, the difference between girls and boys was 7.7 points.
Among children with high cord blood lead, the difference between upper and lower social class was 13.3 points.
Among children with high cord blood lead, low blood lead at 57 months versus high on both occasions corresponded to a 9.1-point GCI difference (+0.42 vs -0.15).
captured_features: postnatal blood lead levels at 6, 12, 18, 24, and 57 months
Mental Development Index (Bayley) score at 24 months
General Cognitive Index (McCarthy) score at 57 months
population: Children followed from birth in a prospective cohort (originally 249; 204 completed 24-month evaluation; 170 evaluated at 57 months, 89.0%) at Children's Hospital, Boston; median assessment age 57.8 months.
exposure_domain: heavy metals (lead), prenatal and postnatal lead exposure
limitations: Regression to the mean influenced the association between initial MDI score and change scores.
Potential measurement artifact from using different testing instruments (Bayley vs McCarthy scales) at the two time points.
Restricted range of prenatal exposure among low and medium cord blood lead groups.
Multicollinearity between predictors required one-stage and two-stage adjustment.
The cohort was relatively socioeconomically advantaged, limiting generalizability to more exposed populations.
Loss to follow-up from the original cohort.
